strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing mixed-type features in tabular generation—an important and largely unaddressed gap
Comprehensive experimental evaluation on 12 diverse datasets with fair baseline comparisons, multiple seeds, and extensive ablation studies demonstrating component contributions
Strong empirical results with 40% average improvement in detection score and consistent gains across multiple metrics (Shape, WD, Trend)
Solid theoretical foundation with formal proof (Theorem 1) that data-dependent coupling tightens transport cost bounds
Modular framework enabling any categorical generative model as low-resolution component, increasing generality
Thorough documentation with detailed appendix covering implementation, additional ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity (Table 20), and qualitative comparisons
Honest treatment of limitations including privacy implications (MIA scores), diversity-fidelity tradeoffs, and simulation methodology
weaknesses: Moderate originality: cascaded framework heavily borrows from image generation literature (Ho et al. 2022); data-dependent couplings from Albergo et al. (2024); overall contribution feels like engineering of existing techniques rather than novel methodology

Theorem 1 has significant limitations: assumes DT encoder and specific data normalization; generalization to GMM encoder and other distributions unclear; absolute bound tightness not established; practical impact on sample quality not empirically validated

Train-test mismatch via teacher forcing: high-resolution model trained on real p_data samples but tested on generated p_low samples; distribution shift not empirically validated as non-problematic, representing potential hidden source of performance degradation
Insufficient analysis of encoder quality sensitivity: switching from DT to GMM causes ~5% detection score drop; no systematic analysis of discretization quality impact on p_high learning

Privacy regression underemphasized: TabCascade MIA scores slightly lower than CDTD (0.959 vs 0.970), indicating higher memorization; for synthetic data generation this is concerning but only briefly acknowledged without solutions
Reduced sample diversity not adequately highlighted: DCR Share of 0.891 with β-Recall of 0.572 suggests lower coverage; fidelity-diversity tradeoff glossed over despite potential practical importance

Experimental concerns: dataset scale mostly <100k rows with unclear scalability; LightGBM sole detection classifier; some hyperparameter choices arbitrary without sensitivity analysis in main results; sampling time ~2.6× slower than CDTD

Presentation issues: 'resolution' terminology for tabular data feels artificial (really just 'categorical easier than numerical'); abstract claims maximum 40% improvement; key algorithm details relegated to appendix; Figure 1 appears twice

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation on 12 datasets with extensive ablations, metrics, and comparisons against 8 baselines—solid empirical methodology
Strong primary results: 40% detection score improvement and >50% WD reduction for numerical features demonstrate practical value
Well-motivated problem: empirical observation (Figure 2a) that categorical features are easier to generate justifies the decomposition approach
Elegant handling of mixed-type features: direct accommodation of missing/inflated values through low-resolution representation (Eq. 2)
Thorough reproducibility: detailed implementation, promised code release, extensive appendices with hyperparameters
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: cascaded diffusion (Ho et al., 2022), data-dependent coupling (Albergo et al., 2024), and learnable schedules (Sahoo et al., 2023) are all from prior work—contribution is mainly combining existing techniques for tabular data

Attribution of improvements unclear: Table 2 shows adding latent z to CDTD alone catastrophically reduces detection score (0.301→0.104), suggesting discretization scheme is problematic and high-resolution FM model compensates, rather than cascade being inherently superior

Forced conceptual framing: the 'resolution' metaphor is not well-justified for tabular data—why is discretized numerical + categorical the natural low-resolution representation? Why not other decompositions?

Design choices lack justification: polynomial degree (5) not justified; max depth (8) appears arbitrary despite sensitivity shown in A.9.4; most learned schedules are nearly linear (Figs 6-17), questioning added complexity

Theorem 1 limitations: only applies to DT encoder; conditions are tautological (MSE minimization is how DT is defined); proof ignores encoder fitting error; practical improvement demonstrated only on 2D toy example (Figure 3)

Mixed metric improvements: while detection/WD improve substantially, diversity (DCR Share 0.884 vs 0.891) and privacy (MIA 0.959 vs 0.970) decrease; α-Precision (0.975 vs 0.971) and β-Recall gains are modest

Experimental concerns: missing values simulated (10% MNAR) not real-world distributions; baselines modified with ad-hoc missing-value mechanisms; teacher forcing creates train-test distribution shift; TabDDPM produces NaNs on multiple datasets

Unclear component contributions: Table 2 indicates improvements come from FM compensating for poor z rather than cascade being fundamental; no ablation isolating cascade benefits independent of FM/schedule choices
Limited analysis of failure modes: tiny improvements on some datasets (electricity: 0.008 vs 0.005); no discussion of when cascade helps vs. hurts or whether joint generation would be preferable

strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation with clear demonstration of the categorical vs. numerical generation difficulty gap (Figure 2) and practical relevance of mixed-type features
Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation across 12 diverse datasets with 13+ metrics, extensive ablation studies, and reproducibility details including promised code release
Substantial empirical improvements: 40% detection score increase over CDTD (0.423 vs 0.301), 50% WD reduction for numerical features, consistent across most datasets
Theoretically grounded approach with Theorem 1 proving data-dependent coupling tightens transport cost bounds; sound mathematical derivations of guided conditional probability paths
Principled handling of mixed-type features via cascaded decomposition with feature-specific masking strategy (Eq. 2) that naturally accommodates missing/inflated values
Honest ablation studies (Table 2) demonstrating necessity of full approach; good presentation of limitations and failure cases
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primary contribution is combining established techniques (cascaded diffusion from Ho et al. 2022, flow matching from Lipman et al. 2023, learnable schedules from CDTD/TabDiff, optimal transport couplings from Albergo et al. 2024) rather than fundamental innovation

Incomplete evaluation of mixed-type features: paper emphasizes missing value handling but lacks comprehensive assessment of zero-inflation and censoring; only simulated MNAR data tested, no real-world missing data experiments

Highly dataset-dependent performance with some datasets showing poor absolute results (electricity: 0.008, news: 0.001 detection scores across all methods); paper lacks analysis of dataset characteristics or failure modes affecting performance

Strong architectural dependency on CDTD as low-resolution model limits modularity; Table 19 shows swapping CDTD for ARF significantly degrades detection score (0.426→0.299), raising questions about whether improvements stem from cascade strategy or CDTD specifically
Encoder selection appears arbitrary: DT outperforms GMM primarily due to more components (65.5 vs 12.5), not fundamental superiority; GMM component cap at 30 seems ad-hoc

Privacy-utility tradeoff insufficiently addressed: MIA scores drop from 0.970 to 0.959 with TabCascade; high-fidelity synthesis risks merit discussion but no comparison with privacy-preserving alternatives
Learned time schedules (Appendix A.6.2) appear mostly linear in practice, questioning necessity of learnable parameterization; no explicit ablation isolating benefits of polynomial vs fixed schedules

Computational overhead underexplored: training two models adds complexity and parameter count; Table 22 shows mixed speed results (slower than some baselines), insufficient discussion of practical tradeoffs

strengths: Novel problem identification: First work to systematically address mixed-type features (discrete point masses + continuous densities) in tabular generation with a principled solution
Strong empirical results: 51.9% improvement in detection score over best baseline (CDTD), with consistent gains across 12 datasets and multiple evaluation metrics
Theoretical contribution: Formal proof (Theorem 1) that data-dependent coupling tightens transport cost bounds, providing theoretical justification
Well-motivated cascaded decomposition: Empirically supported observation (Figure 2a) that categorical features are easier to learn than numerical ones
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 12 diverse datasets, multiple baselines, numerous metrics, detailed ablation studies, fair implementation with aligned architectures
Technical soundness: Proper derivations, novel guided conditional probability paths with closed-form solutions, feature-specific learnable time schedules
Practical relevance: Addresses missing values, zero inflation, and censoring—problems existing methods cannot generate
Excellent reproducibility: Detailed implementation info, promised code release, extensive appendix with additional experiments and analysis
weaknesses: Incremental technical novelty: Primarily combines existing techniques (cascaded diffusion from Ho et al. 2022, flow matching from Lipman et al. 2023, data-dependent couplings from Albergo et al. 2024); Theorem 1 is straightforward application of coupling theory

Strong dependency on CDTD: Performance substantially drops when switching low-resolution model to ARF (detection 0.782→0.494 in Table 23), indicating unclear contribution of cascade vs. choice of low-res model; CDTD itself already achieves 0.518 detection

Arbitrary conceptual justification for 'resolution': Low/high-res decomposition is empirically motivated but lacks deep theoretical justification; alternative decompositions (by correlation, causality, etc.) unexplored

Increased complexity vs. baselines: Multi-stage pipeline with encoder pre-training, two models, and multiple hyperparameters; dependency on forked R package (disttree) via rpy2; Table 24 shows sensitivity to encoder complexity (range 0.66-0.78)
Limited novelty in mixed-type handling: Once z encodes discrete states, mechanism is relatively straightforward; solution is pragmatic (masking losses) rather than principled
Privacy-utility tradeoff underexplored: MIA scores notably lower than CDTD (0.935 vs. 0.958), indicating higher privacy risk; encoder complexity tradeoff (Table 24) insufficiently analyzed

Insufficient analysis of applicability: No clear characterization of dataset characteristics favoring the method; variance in improvements across datasets not explained (detection ranges 0.202-0.891 in Table 4)
Limited encoder exploration: Only DT vs. GMM compared; Theorem 1 specifically requires DT encoder, limiting theoretical generality; no neural discretization methods explored
Presentation density: Notation heavy in Section 4.2, connection between components unclear; 'resolution' terminology used before formally defined

Experimental limitations: Artificially simulated MNAR missing values may not reflect real-world patterns; datasets small-to-medium sized; no high-dimensional experiments; limited characterization of when cascading helps most
